subproblem.title: Operator norm is at most the Hilbert-Schmidt norm, and the Hilbert-Schmidt norm is continuous
subproblem.statement: For all natural numbers m, k >= 0: every continuous linear map A : R^m -> R^k satisfies ||A|| <= hsNorm(A), where ||A|| is the operator norm and hsNorm(A) = (sum_{i<m} ||A e_i||^2)^(1/2) is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm (e_i the standard orthonormal basis of R^m). Moreover the map A -> hsNorm(A) is continuous on the space L(R^m, R^k) of continuous linear maps with its operator-norm topology.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (m k : ℕ), (∀ A : Rn m →L[ℝ] Rn k, ‖A‖ ≤ hsNorm A) ∧ Continuous (fun A : Rn m →L[ℝ] Rn k => hsNorm A)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 1 of the parent proof (Hilbert-Schmidt versus operator norm), for arbitrary dimensions m, k.

Notation.
- L := L(R^m, R^k) is the space of continuous linear maps R^m -> R^k. It carries the operator norm ||T||, the least C >= 0 with ||T v|| <= C ||v|| for all v, and the topology of this norm.
- e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1 (i < m) is the standard orthonormal basis of R^m.
- By definition hsNormSq(T) = sum_{i<m} ||T e_i||^2 and hsNorm(T) = Real.sqrt(hsNormSq(T)). In particular hsNorm(T) >= 0.

1. Fix T in L and v in R^m with coordinates v_i (i < m). Expanding v in the standard orthonormal basis gives v = sum_{i<m} v_i e_i ((EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin m) R).sum_repr v). Also ||v|| = sqrt(sum_{i<m} |v_i|^2) (EuclideanSpace.norm_eq).

2. By linearity, T v = sum_i v_i T e_i. By the triangle inequality for finite sums and ||v_i T e_i|| = |v_i| ||T e_i||, we get ||T v|| <= sum_i |v_i| ||T e_i||.

3. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums of reals reads sum_i a_i b_i <= sqrt(sum_i a_i^2) sqrt(sum_i b_i^2) (Real.sum_mul_le_sqrt_mul_sqrt). Apply it with a_i = |v_i| and b_i = ||T e_i||: sum_i |v_i| ||T e_i|| <= sqrt(sum_i |v_i|^2) sqrt(sum_i ||T e_i||^2) = ||v|| hsNorm(T), using step 1 and the definition of hsNorm.

4. By steps 2 and 3, ||T v|| <= hsNorm(T) ||v|| for every v in R^m. Since hsNorm(T) >= 0, the operator-norm bound criterion (ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_le_bound) gives ||T|| <= hsNorm(T). If m = 0, all sums are empty and the same argument applies verbatim: v = 0 and every quantity above is 0.

5. Continuity. For each i < m, the evaluation T -> T e_i is a continuous linear map L -> R^k (ContinuousLinearMap.apply R (Rn k) e_i). So T -> ||T e_i||^2 is continuous, as a composition with the continuous norm and with squaring. Hence T -> hsNormSq(T) = sum_{i<m} ||T e_i||^2 is continuous as a finite sum of continuous real functions (continuous_finsetSum). Then T -> hsNorm(T) = sqrt(hsNormSq(T)) is continuous as its composition with the continuous function Real.sqrt.

6. Steps 4 and 5 hold for arbitrary m, k and T in L, and they are exactly the two conjuncts of the statement.
proof_key_steps: Expand v = sum_i v_i e_i; linearity and the triangle inequality give ||T v|| <= sum_i |v_i| ||T e_i||
Cauchy-Schwarz for finite sums: sum_i |v_i| ||T e_i|| <= ||v|| hsNorm(T), using ||v|| = sqrt(sum_i |v_i|^2)
ContinuousLinearMap.opNorm_le_bound with the nonnegative constant hsNorm(T) gives ||T|| <= hsNorm(T)
hsNorm = sqrt of a finite sum of squared norms of the continuous evaluations T -> T e_i, hence continuous

audit.reason: The one-line Lean proposition matches both prose conclusions for arbitrary natural dimensions. Independently checked all proof steps: basis expansion, linearity, the finite-sum triangle inequality, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the nonnegative operator-norm bound establish the first conjunct, including dimension zero. Continuous evaluations, squared norms, finite summation, and continuous square root establish the second. The proof is complete, non-circular, and directly formalizable. Its unreserved bare name and standalone type satisfy the comparator requirements.

subproblem.title: Continuous extension, with the same Hoelder modulus, of an operator-valued map from a dense subset
subproblem.statement: Let n, m, k >= 0, let F : R^n -> L(R^m, R^k) be any map into the continuous linear maps R^m -> R^k (operator-norm topology), let S and Z be subsets of R^n, and let M, R, alpha be reals with M >= 0, R > 0 and alpha > 0. Assume S is contained in the closure of Z, and hsNorm(F(x) - F(y)) <= M (||x - y||/R)^alpha for all x, y in Z, where hsNorm is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Then there is g : R^n -> L(R^m, R^k) with three properties: g is continuous on S; g(x) = F(x) for every x in Z; and hsNorm(g(x) - g(y)) <= M (||x - y||/R)^alpha for all x, y in S.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (n m k : ℕ) (F : Rn n → (Rn m →L[ℝ] Rn k)) (S Z : Set (Rn n)) (M R α : ℝ), 0 ≤ M → 0 < R → 0 < α → S ⊆ closure Z → (∀ x ∈ Z, ∀ y ∈ Z, hsNorm (F x - F y) ≤ M * (‖x - y‖ / R) ^ α) → ∃ g : Rn n → (Rn m →L[ℝ] Rn k), ContinuousOn g S ∧ (∀ x ∈ Z, g x = F x) ∧ ∀ x ∈ S, ∀ y ∈ S, hsNorm (g x - g y) ≤ M * (‖x - y‖ / R) ^ α
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: steps 3 and 4 of the parent proof, with an arbitrary map F in place of Df and an arbitrary set S contained in the closure of Z in place of the ball B. The comparison of step 1 is supplied by the sibling child hs_norm_basics. The density of Z in B is step 2 of the parent proof and is proved in the parent.

Notation.
- L := L(R^m, R^k) is the space of continuous linear maps R^m -> R^k with the operator norm ||.||. L is complete, because its codomain R^k is complete. As a normed space it is Hausdorff and regular.
- kappa(t) := M (t/R)^alpha for real t (real power). The hypothesis then reads hsNorm(F x - F y) <= kappa(||x - y||) for x, y in Z.
- For x in R^n, nhdsWithin x Z denotes the filter of neighbourhoods of x within Z.
- The sibling child hs_norm_basics (allard52_c1h_opNorm_le_hsNorm_continuous with these m, k) gives:
  (HS1) ||T|| <= hsNorm(T) for every T in L;
  (HS2) T -> hsNorm(T) is continuous on L.

1. Properties of kappa.
- Since alpha >= 0, t -> t^alpha is continuous on R (Real.continuous_rpow_const). So kappa is continuous: compose with t -> t/R, then multiply by the constant M.
- Since alpha != 0, 0^alpha = 0 (Real.zero_rpow), so kappa(0) = 0.
- kappa is nondecreasing on [0, infinity). If 0 <= s <= t, then 0 <= s/R <= t/R because R > 0, so (s/R)^alpha <= (t/R)^alpha (Real.rpow_le_rpow, exponent alpha >= 0). Multiplying by M >= 0 gives kappa(s) <= kappa(t).

2. Small modulus. For every epsilon > 0 there is eta > 0 with kappa(2 eta) < epsilon. The function eta -> kappa(2 eta) is continuous (step 1) and takes the value kappa(0) = 0 at eta = 0. So there is delta > 0 with |kappa(2 eta)| < epsilon whenever |eta| < delta, and eta := delta/2 > 0 works.

3. Limits along Z exist. Let x be in closure Z.
- nhdsWithin x Z is a nontrivial filter (mem_closure_iff_nhdsWithin_neBot), hence so is its image under F.
- The image filter is Cauchy (Metric.cauchy_iff). Given epsilon > 0, take eta from step 2 and t := F(Z cap B^o_eta(x)). Then t belongs to the image filter, because Z cap B^o_eta(x) belongs to nhdsWithin x Z.
- For z, z' in Z cap B^o_eta(x) we have ||z - z'|| <= ||z - x|| + ||z' - x|| < 2 eta. Hence dist(F z, F z') = ||F z - F z'|| <= hsNorm(F z - F z') <= kappa(||z - z'||) <= kappa(2 eta) < epsilon. This uses (HS1), the hypothesis (z, z' are in Z), and the monotonicity of kappa on [0, infinity) from step 1.
- Since L is complete, the Cauchy image filter converges (cauchy_map_iff_exists_tendsto). So there is y in L with F(z) -> y as z -> x within Z.

4. Definition of g. Let g := extendFrom Z F; that is, g(x) is a chosen limit of F along nhdsWithin x Z whenever such a limit exists. By step 3 and tendsto_extendFrom:
(*) for every x in closure Z, F(z) -> g(x) as z -> x within Z.

5. g is continuous on S. S is contained in closure Z, and by step 3, F has a limit along nhdsWithin x Z at every x in S. Since L is a regular space, continuousOn_extendFrom shows that g is continuous on S.

6. g = F on Z. Let x be in Z, so x is in closure Z.
- For every z in Z, 0 <= ||F z - F x|| <= hsNorm(F z - F x) <= kappa(||z - x||), by (HS1) and the hypothesis.
- The function z -> kappa(||z - x||) is continuous and equals kappa(0) = 0 at z = x. So kappa(||z - x||) -> 0 as z -> x, in particular along nhdsWithin x Z, which is finer than the neighbourhood filter of x.
- By the squeeze theorem (squeeze_zero'), ||F z - F x|| -> 0 along nhdsWithin x Z. That is, F(z) -> F(x) as z -> x within Z (tendsto_iff_norm_sub_tendsto_zero).
- As x is in closure Z and limits in the Hausdorff space L are unique, extendFrom_eq gives g(x) = F(x).

7. Hoelder bound on S. Let x, y be in S. Both nhdsWithin x Z and nhdsWithin y Z are nontrivial, since x and y are in closure Z. Hence the product filter Phi := (nhdsWithin x Z) x (nhdsWithin y Z) on R^n x R^n is nontrivial.
(a) Composing (*) for x and for y with the two projections gives F(p_1) - F(p_2) -> g(x) - g(y) along Phi. So by (HS2), hsNorm(F(p_1) - F(p_2)) -> hsNorm(g(x) - g(y)) along Phi.
(b) Phi is finer than the product of the neighbourhood filters of x and y, which is the neighbourhood filter of (x, y). The map p -> kappa(||p_1 - p_2||) is continuous (step 1). So kappa(||p_1 - p_2||) -> kappa(||x - y||) along Phi.
(c) Z x Z belongs to Phi, and for p in Z x Z the hypothesis gives hsNorm(F(p_1) - F(p_2)) <= kappa(||p_1 - p_2||).
A non-strict inequality that holds eventually passes to limits along a nontrivial filter (le_of_tendsto_of_tendsto). Applied to (a), (b) and (c), this gives hsNorm(g(x) - g(y)) <= kappa(||x - y||) = M (||x - y||/R)^alpha.

8. Steps 5, 6 and 7 show that this g satisfies all three conclusions. No case distinction is needed: if S or Z is empty, the corresponding clauses are vacuous.
proof_key_steps: kappa(t) = M (t/R)^alpha is continuous, nondecreasing on [0, infinity) and kappa(0) = 0, so kappa(2 eta) < epsilon for some eta > 0
For x in closure Z, nhdsWithin x Z is nontrivial and its image under F is Cauchy (||.|| <= hsNorm, hypothesis, monotonicity of kappa), hence convergent in the complete space L
g := extendFrom Z F satisfies F -> g(x) along nhdsWithin x Z on closure Z and is continuous on S by continuousOn_extendFrom
For x in Z, F(z) -> F(x) within Z by the squeeze theorem, so g(x) = F(x) by extendFrom_eq
Passing to the limit along (nhdsWithin x Z) x (nhdsWithin y Z) in hsNorm(F p1 - F p2) <= kappa(||p1 - p2||), using continuity of hsNorm and kappa, gives the Hoelder bound on S

audit.reason: The exact Lean proposition includes every prose hypothesis and all three conclusions, including agreement on all of Z. Independently checked the modulus properties, positive small-radius choice, nontrivial Cauchy image filters, completeness, extendFrom construction, continuity on S, agreement on Z by squeezing and uniqueness, and passage of the inequality through a nontrivial product filter. Each hypothesis is used correctly; empty sets and zero dimensions cause no gap. The sole child dependency, hs_norm_basics, is correctly directed and non-circular. The unreserved bare name and standalone type are valid. Together with density and the parent's declared differentiability sibling, these conclusions establish exactly the selected parent's C¹ and Hölder conclusions.
